waveTitle: The alignment engine, measured for the first time and then fixed

pieces.name: Document model & block identity
pieces.scope: ProseMirror schema shaped like OOXML; stable anchors that ride transactions
pieces.evidence: 5/5 identity tests pass: typing preserves anchors, split keeps identity on the first half, paste de-duplicates, delete is clean
pieces.gap: Not yet exercised against a real .docx-derived document.

pieces.name: App shell & host seam
pieces.scope: React chrome, ProseMirror surface, bun server implementing HostApi
pieces.evidence: The app runs. Real .md opened from disk, edited and saved back correctly — frontmatter, GFM table, ordered list, bold, em-dash, CJK and ± all survived. Live status bar reads 2.7 ms p99 keystroke latency in a real browser, including ProseMirror’s DOM write, against an 8 ms budget.
pieces.gap: Only the Markdown path is wired. Opening a .docx in the app is not possible yet, so the document-polish comparison against Google Docs cannot be run.

pieces.name: Markdown ⇄ model
pieces.evidence: Link hrefs lost across 1,437 real documents: 4, all CommonMark spec cases with backslash escapes inside URLs. Images are inline nodes, so a linked badge keeps its href and a mid-sentence image no longer splits its paragraph.
pieces.gap: A no-op save still rewrites 64% of lines across the corpus — mostly escaping of “_” and “*”, which cannot be narrowed without risking a change to what reparses as emphasis.

pieces.name: docx import, sidecar & anchors
pieces.scope: Offset-recording XML index, fidelity sidecar, alignment-based re-anchoring
pieces.evidence: 288/288 real Word documents import; mean text recovery 99.49%. The re-anchoring engine — 925 lines of constrained Needleman–Wunsch, what the design calls “the actual research problem” — now has a test, and it found a traceback bug worth ~40 points of recall on every position-changing edit. Across 12 documents and ~5,600 blocks per scenario: reword, rewrite, split, merge, insert and delete all recover 100%; a moved section 95.7%; a week of every kind of edit at once 93.8%. Reproducible run to run.
pieces.gap: Moves are the honest limit: a move is not expressible in an order-preserving alignment, so it is recovered afterwards by exact content match, which a block that was moved AND reworded defeats. Those 239 blocks are lost and ledgered, never guessed at. Text inside text boxes and content controls is still dropped.

pieces.name: Round-trip scorer & corpus
pieces.scope: Real-world .docx corpus, three-tier fidelity score, pandoc baseline
pieces.evidence: Three tiers over 288 files with a pandoc baseline, plus an anti-strawman control: pandoc scored against its OWN output reaches 0.9743, so it is self-consistent and simply does not preserve the user’s document. Independently re-verified outside the scorer, including that pandoc can read our exported files with the edit intact.
pieces.gap: T2 is entailed by T0 for scriv and is labelled as such in the report rather than counted as a second result.

pieces.name: Latency gate
pieces.scope: Keystroke budget enforced by a test that fails the build
pieces.evidence: Every row in ARCHITECTURE §5 is now measured. Keystroke→paint runs in real Chromium on the app's own plugin stack and stylesheets, with three independent trace methods. Baseline recorded on a quiet machine. GATE: pass on two consecutive runs.
pieces.gap: “Off main thread” for diagnostics is asserted structurally, not observed — proving no long task lands during a refresh needs a PerformanceObserver in the browser harness.

pieces.name: Smart text ops
pieces.scope: Selection-aware surrounds, multi-cursor, motions, transpose, join, kill-line
pieces.evidence: Multi-cursor works in the app: Cmd-D three times over a term gives three cursors and typing replaces all three at once — the “rename a term consistently” step of the comparison task, in one action, at 1.9 ms. 60 package tests.
pieces.gap: IME composition is not multiplexed across cursors, and column selection is not built.

pieces.name: Prose IntelliSense
pieces.scope: Workspace symbol index, completions, Harper diagnostics over an LSP seam
pieces.evidence: Completion gated at 0.78 ms p99 against 3,775 symbols from 93 workspace documents. Diagnostics gated at 40 ms p99 (budget 150) — incremental, cancellable, one block re-checked per edit. 11 new tests hold the incremental linter to the whole-document result on real corpus prose.
pieces.gap: Harper reads `Node.js` as a sentence end, so `js` is a misspelling and the next word 'does not start with a capital'. That cascade is most of what remains on technical documents. A user dictionary and per-rule ignores are the answer and are not built.

pieces.name: AI inline edit
pieces.scope: Cmd-K streaming rewrite as accept/reject diff; three-way merge; agent mode
pieces.evidence: Cmd-K works in the app: opens on a selection, and with no key configured reports which environment variable to set while everything else keeps working. Suggestion rendering verified without a key via CriticMarkup, which parses to the same marks. 29 package tests; 135 across the repo.
pieces.gap: The live provider round trip is still unverified: there is no API key in this environment, so Cmd-K streaming and agent mode's model layer have never been run against a real model. The deterministic half of agent mode needs no model and is tested against 120 real corpus documents.

pieces.name: Workspace & git
pieces.scope: Fuzzy open, search, diff and blame at sentence granularity
pieces.evidence: The changes pane renders sentence diff and blame; Cmd-Shift-G toggles it. Against a real repo with a reorder, a reword and a reflow made together, git says “4 insertions, 2 deletions” while ours says “1 reworded · 1 removed · 1 split”, labels each change with its section, and shows the reword at word level. The reflow contributes nothing.
pieces.gap: A sentence that is BOTH moved and reworded is not recognised as a move — pure reorderings are, but combining the two makes the aligner fall back to removed-plus-split. Blame renders but has not been exercised against a repo with multiple authors.

pieces.name: docx export splice
pieces.scope: Edit the original zip rather than regenerate it
pieces.evidence: The comparison task’s terminology rename, run on a real 801 KB consultation document with comment threads — 1,161 paragraphs, 8,200 words. The term changed in 44 places; 1 of 20 zip parts changed; 33 of 1,186 paragraphs differ. comments.xml, styles.xml, numbering.xml and settings.xml all come back BYTE-IDENTICAL, and pandoc reads the result.
pieces.gap: New comments (as against replies) are not written: a new thread needs an arbitrary range spliced into the body rather than one copied from a parent.

pieces.name: Comments
pieces.scope: Read Word’s thread structure; reply and resolve, written back into the four annotation parts
pieces.evidence: Blind-comparison task step 5 runs end to end on a real Word document and was verified by opening the saved file: 30 of 34 parts byte-identical, the reply threaded under its parent, the parent marked done. 8 round-trip tests against real corpus files.
pieces.gap: Creating a new comment on a selection is not built. Markdown comments are CriticMarkup, which cannot carry an author, a thread or a resolved state — the panel disables reply/resolve there and says so.

pieces.name: Fidelity panel
pieces.scope: What this document loses on the way in, and what a save would actually write
pieces.evidence: Runs a real export on demand and throws it away, so the answer is what would be written rather than an estimate. On a 452-block RFP: unedited, 0 of 29 parts rewritten and byte-identical; one word typed, 1 of 29 parts and 1 block rebuilt.
pieces.gap: No jump-to-block from a ledger entry yet: an entry names an `aid` but clicking it does not move the caret there.

pieces.name: Agent mode
pieces.scope: An instruction that edits the whole workspace, reviewed site by site before it lands
pieces.evidence: Verified end to end in the running app on 1,492 files. Edits the file at byte offsets rather than regenerating it, so a one-word rename is a one-word diff. Sites flagged uncertain start rejected; the apply re-reads every file and skips sites that moved during review. 18 tests against 120 real corpus documents.
pieces.gap: Only the rename instruction is built. Turning free-form natural language into a change set needs the model layer, which is unwired because there is no provider key here — claiming a round trip I have not seen would be worse than naming the boundary.

metrics.label: Keystroke → state commit
metrics.note: Now measured against the app's own 17-plugin stack via apps/web/src/perf-plugins.ts. Every earlier keystroke number on this page was measured against aidPlugin + history — two plugins out of seventeen.

metrics.label: Keystroke → paint, end to end
metrics.note: Measured at last: the Playwright/CDP harness existed and was imported by nothing. First real number was 17.0 ms — over budget — and the gate would not act on it because 240 samples put only 3 behind the p99. Samples raised to 900, then fixed: `content-visibility: auto` on top-level blocks took p50 from 11.09 to 6.00 ms and p99 from 17.82 to 11.65. Three independent trace methods, real Chromium, the app's own plugin stack and stylesheets.

metrics.label: Diagnostics refresh
metrics.note: Was 7,846 ms when the whole document was re-linted on every keystroke. Now one block is re-checked per edit (p50 and p99 both 1 block) and the other 1,236 come from a content-keyed cache. In the running app on a 17k-word document: 27 ms, then 12 ms.

metrics.label: Link targets lost, 1437 files
metrics.note: Shown red because it is: the budget is 0 and the figure is 4. This tile used to render green — the page inferred budget direction from the unit, and for a count where fewer is better the comparison ran backwards.

metrics.label: Completion popup open
metrics.note: Against 3,775 symbols from 93 real workspace documents. Runs inside state.apply on every keystroke whether or not the popup opens, so it is also gated at a 2 ms p50.

metrics.label: Diagnostics blocks re-checked per edit
metrics.note: p50 and p99 alike. This is the design claim of the incremental linter, asserted rather than assumed.

metrics.label: Squiggles drawn inside code
metrics.note: On a 17,083-word Node.js API document the checker drew 2,986 marks and 1,469 sat inside code blocks. `beforeExit` is not a misspelling. Code is masked to spaces before the checker sees it — same length, so every offset still maps. That document: 2,986 → 548 marks.

metrics.label: Cold scan, 40k words
metrics.note: The first pass over a whole document, reported and deliberately not gated: §5 budgets the refresh a writer feels while typing, not the open. Results stream in from the top as they are computed rather than the page staying blank.

metrics.label: Word parts untouched on a comment reply
metrics.note: Reply posted and thread resolved on a real 7-thread Word document, then the saved file was opened and compared. Only comments.xml, commentsExtended.xml, commentsIds.xml and document.xml differ — and document.xml grew by 101 characters, the reply’s range and nothing else.

metrics.label: Corpus documents carrying comments
metrics.note: And not one of them has a reply or a resolution. That is why the round-trip test writes its own: there is nothing in the world’s .docx files here to read back.

metrics.label: Keystroke → paint, median
metrics.note: Was 11.09 ms. ProseMirror renders every block of the document; content-visibility is the browser’s own viewport virtualization, so the editor never has to know.

metrics.label: Word parts rewritten, one-word edit
metrics.note: Shown to the writer in the fidelity panel before they send the file: 451 of 452 blocks copied verbatim, 1 rebuilt. Checked in 69 ms by running a real export and throwing it away.

metrics.label: Agent rename precision
metrics.note: "Zephyrine"→"Halcyon" across a 1,492-file workspace. Exactly the 12 prose occurrences were proposed; the fenced block, the inline `zephyrine()`, the `require("zephyrine")` and the URL in a link destination were all left alone. Applied — and the diff against the original 559-line file was the block seeded for the test and nothing else.

metrics.label: Agent sites found, real term
metrics.note: "configuration"→"setup": 118 exact, 34 variant, 0 needing a decision. Grouped by file, every site showing its line, accept/reject per site.

metrics.label: Anchor recall, insert or delete
metrics.note: Was 61%. A writer edits a file in vim or pulls a colleague's PR, and every paragraph's Word formatting, comments and revisions have to find their way back. Insertions and deletions now cost only the paragraphs they touch.

metrics.label: Anchor recall, a week of editing
metrics.note: Reword, split, insert, delete and a moved section, all applied to the same document. Was 52.7%.

metrics.label: Blocks silently misapplied
metrics.note: The failure that actually matters: one paragraph wearing another's Word properties, with nothing on screen to say so. Insert and delete each misapplied 2 before this wave and now misapply none. Against these 3 sit 339 blocks that were safely lost — visible, ledgered, recoverable. The engine fails in the right direction.

metrics.label: Aligner alone, no move recovery
metrics.note: Was ~10% on any document past 200 blocks. The exact-content recovery pass runs after the alignment and was carrying the entire feature; turning it off is what made the defect visible. This number is checked by a test that needs no corpus, so it still runs on a fresh clone.

metrics.label: Aids that break key order
metrics.note: 1,235 block ids across the whole corpus come out as all-digit strings, and JavaScript hoists integer-like keys to the front of an object regardless of insertion order. So `Object.keys(blocks)` is not document order — about one block in a hundred moves, and a different few on every import, because the ids are random.

decisions.d: ProseMirror, used directly — not Tiptap, not Lexical
decisions.why: Pure decorations are load-bearing for AI diffs, diagnostics and blame. Lexical and Quill lack them; Tiptap's auto-schema fights the OOXML mapping.

decisions.d: Splice the original zip; never regenerate it
decisions.why: Turns 'how much OOXML can we model?' into 'how little must we touch?'. An unedited round-trip is byte-identical, and fidelity degrades only in proportion to what was actually edited.

decisions.d: Exact in-session, fuzzy only for externally-edited files
decisions.why: While the doc is open we observed every change, so identity needs no guessing. Sequence alignment is reserved for files edited by another tool — that split is what makes the problem tractable.

decisions.d: Drop formatting rather than risk misapplying it
decisions.why: A dropped style is a visible bug the writer can fix; a misapplied one silently corrupts a document they trusted.

decisions.d: harper.js in a worker, behind an LSP-shaped seam
decisions.why: Offline, Apache-2.0, works unchanged in web v1 and Tauri v2. The LSP shape makes adding a second checker cheap.

decisions.d: A measurement that covers only part of a path may fail a budget but may never certify a pass
decisions.why: A headless process cannot see the DOM half of a keystroke. Reporting it as 'pass' would manufacture confidence in a number that never measured the thing it names.

decisions.d: A tier entailed by another tier is labelled, not counted twice
decisions.why: Scriv’s T2 is 1.0000 because T0 is 100% — T2 scores the zero-edit round trip that T0 already proved byte-identical. Presenting both as achievements would inflate one fact into two.

decisions.d: A budget that names a size needs an upper bound on the band, and warm-up is reported separately rather than folded in
decisions.why: “50-page” measured as “≥500 paragraphs” swept in 11,000-paragraph documents and reported a failure three times the real one; a bench with no warm-up puts JIT cost in the p99 tail and blames the code for it.

decisions.d: Verified by pressing them in the running app, not by reading a table
decisions.why: Mod-Ctrl-ArrowUp looked ideal for expand-selection and is silently eaten by Mission Control on macOS. The keys the OS takes are now listed in the binding table so they are not rediscovered.

decisions.d: Every package is a referenced project, not just the ones that happened to be listed
decisions.why: Four packages including the largest were outside the root tsconfig references, so every clean typecheck was checking a subset. Adding them surfaced 114 errors, three of which were real defects.

decisions.d: The popup never opens on a bare word, at any length
decisions.why: Every threshold low enough to be useful is low enough to interrupt an ordinary sentence. Code completion can fire on every identifier character because a programmer is always naming something; a writer usually is not.

decisions.d: The gate will not fail on a percentile its own sample size cannot support
decisions.why: docx throughput measured 1.299, 1.841 and 2.281 ms across three runs of identical code. With 227 samples a p99 rests on about three order statistics. A gate that fails at random teaches people to re-run until it passes.

decisions.d: Rendered with the schema’s existing tracked-change marks, not a parallel mechanism
decisions.why: Accepting an AI rewrite and accepting a colleague’s tracked change become one code path, an AI suggestion exports to Word as a real revision, and undo and position mapping already understand it.

decisions.d: Squiggles are decorations, and the checker declines languages it cannot handle
decisions.why: A squiggle in the document would be savable, undoable and exportable to Word. And running an English checker over Hindi produces a wall of false errors, which is worse than no diagnostics at all.

decisions.d: A newline inside a block is a soft wrap, not a sentence boundary
decisions.why: Treating it as one made reflowing a paragraph produce a diff — defeating the entire purpose — and hid every mixed-authorship sentence from blame, since each fragment sat on its own line.

decisions.d: The primary cursor stays a real selection; extra cursors are plugin state drawn as decorations
decisions.why: A Selection subclass holding N ranges is the “proper” answer and breaks everything downstream — the view draws one native selection, and baseKeymap, input rules and mark logic all read the primary range.

decisions.d: Inline, not block
decisions.why: Markdown’s linked badge is a link wrapping an image and OOXML’s drawing sits inside a run. Modelling images as blocks forced every in-paragraph image to split it, and the enclosing link mark had nowhere to live — so saving a file deleted the hyperlink.

decisions.d: Derived from the binding table, not maintained beside it
decisions.why: Thirty text operations had a key and no palette entry, and two of them were bound to chords macOS eats — so they could not be invoked at all. Deriving the palette from the table means a binding cannot exist without being discoverable.

decisions.d: Losing a match and misapplying one are counted separately and held to different standards
decisions.why: They are not the same size of mistake. A lost anchor loses formatting visibly, says so in the ledger, and the writer can fix it. A misapplied one hands one paragraph another's properties and says nothing. A single “accuracy” number would let the second hide inside the first.

decisions.d: Never read it from an object's key order
decisions.why: Block ids are random per import and about 1% come out looking like integers, which JavaScript hoists to the front. The alignment engine was being scored against documents whose paragraphs had been shuffled, with numbers that drifted between runs.

decisions.d: Measure each layer with the layer beneath it switched off
decisions.why: A recovery pass that runs after the aligner made a broken aligner look like a merely underperforming one at 61%. With it disabled the real figure was 10%, and the cause was findable in an afternoon.

notes: The alignment engine had no test at all — 925 lines of constrained Needleman–Wunsch, and beside it a 239-line ground-truth harness built for exactly this purpose that was imported by nothing. The expensive half of making it checkable had already been done and never used.

Its first measurement found the bug. The traceback decided whether a gap had been opened or extended by testing a Float32 cell for equality within 1e-6, on a matrix whose values reach several hundred where one ulp is ~6e-5 — sixty times coarser than the tolerance. The test could not come out true, so a traceback that entered a gap never left it. One five-paragraph insertion 66 blocks from the end turned the rest of the walk into 5,382 consecutive inserts and ran the column index to -4758; every earlier anchor was reported lost.

The alignment itself was never wrong. Instrumented on a 669-block document, the optimum score is reached along the true path, with true-pair similarity at p50 0.981 and displacement well inside the band. Every match was there to be taken. Only the walk back was broken — which is why the symptom looked like a scoring problem and stayed unexplained for a wave.

A test that cannot fail is not a test, so each new one was run against the old code first. The aligner test turns 4 of its 7 red, including the mirror-image defect on deletions at “20.3%, 240 lost”. The block-order test binds a comment to “Fourth paragraph.” instead of “First paragraph.”

Two numbers in this project's own bug report were wrong, both from measuring a 12-document sample instead of the corpus. Integer-like block ids are 0.94%, not 0.07% — one block in a hundred, not one in 1,500. And the comment-binding bug it described is latent rather than active: it needs one comment anchor in two blocks, which happens zero times across all 288 documents. The fix is still right; the report overstated what it was fixing.

Measurements taken while files are being edited are not measurements. Two corpus runs disagreed — 5,406 blocks against 5,405 — and both were contaminated by edits landing mid-run. Sorting document order out made three consecutive clean runs byte-identical, which is the only reason the numbers on this page can be quoted.

This page was rendering a failing tile green. Budget direction was inferred from the unit, so for a count where fewer is better the comparison ran backwards: 4 link targets lost against a budget of 0 read as a pass. build.ts's own comment says a progress page that shows green while the gate is failing is worse than no page.

Four test files were passing with zero assertions when the corpus is absent — and the corpus is gitignored, so that is the state of a fresh clone. The worst had a guard that read `expect(true).toBe(true)`, in the one file that checks the byte-identity targets. New tests for the aligner and for block order need no corpus at all.

Theme cycling was dead. `view.cycleTheme` and `table.insert` were both on ⌘⌥T, the later registration wins, and `table.insert` is live whenever the caret is in the document — so the binding did nothing exactly when anyone would use it. I introduced it myself, moving the theme off another chord. The whole binding table is now read by a test that fails on any collision.

Heading numbering is built and deliberately not shown. 37 corpus documents auto-number their headings and none of it reached the editor; the engine scores 57.2% against the numbers Word itself cached in 14 documents' tables of contents, up from 5.3% once numbering was read off the paragraph style rather than the paragraph. A wrong section number is worse than a missing one, so it stays dark until that number is much higher.

Agent mode's rename needs no model, and that is the design rather than a limitation. Word boundaries, plurals, possessives, case and "never touch code" are all decidable; deciding them exactly is more useful than asking a model to guess, and it means the feature works with the network unplugged.

The rename's own test caught the bug that would have destroyed a workspace: `classify` extends a site to carry a plural but returned only the term's end, so `to` sat one suffix short of `before` — every carried site would have written "settingss" over "configurations".

The keystroke→paint harness was complete, well-designed, and imported by nothing — a whole subsystem with a row in the report and no caller. Wired up, it failed: 17.0 ms against a 16 ms budget. And the gate would not act on it, because 240 samples put only 3 behind the p99. A budget that can never fail is not a budget.

ProseMirror renders every block; CodeMirror-based editors virtualize the viewport. That is the bill for the tree model that makes decorations and the docx mapping tractable. `content-visibility: auto` is the browser's own version of that virtualization — p50 11.09 → 6.00 ms — and the obvious risk, that it makes jumping to the end of a long document expensive, was measured both ways and is not real.

spliceZip was eating its own input. `buf.slice(...)` on a Node Buffer is the legacy alias for `subarray` and yields a VIEW, so patching the central directory wrote straight back into the caller's bytes. The exported package was always correct and the ORIGIN was destroyed. Invisible with a plain Uint8Array, where `.slice()` copies — which is exactly why it survived.

The importer hard-coded `resolved: false, parentAnchorId: null` and never opened commentsExtended.xml. Every reply in every document would have read as a separate top-level thread. The corpus hid it completely: 675 threads across 11 documents, and not one carries a reply or a resolution.

The global key dispatcher listens in the capture phase on window, so it saw every key before any text field did: ⌘⏎ in the comment reply box ran “Exit code block”, and ⌘B in the search field toggled bold in the document behind it.

OffsetMap was wrong and a new test caught it. It emitted a separator for every BLOCK; textBetween emits one only before a TEXTBLOCK. A bullet list with four items is nine blocks and four textblocks — so in any document containing a list, every diagnostic, every AI hunk and every extra cursor after the first list landed on the wrong word. Nothing threw.

The incremental linter was expected to match a whole-document lint exactly. On real prose it does not — 4 diagnostics in 200 — and the difference runs the other way: Harper does not treat a bare newline as a sentence end, so the joined document merged two speakers' dialogue into one '52-word sentence' warning while hiding three real findings inside the paragraphs it had glued together.
Making images render broke the splice engine — T0 fell from 60/60 byte-identical to 54/60 — and the assertion added an hour earlier caught it. That is what a gate is for.

An independent audit found two of four house rules violated, a security defect, and the headline fidelity metric ungated. It was right on all three. The worst: saving an unedited Markdown file was DELETING hyperlinks from CI badges — silent data loss in the layer this project calls the source of truth. I had seen the symptom myself, filed it as a pre-existing limitation, and moved on.

Move detection had never fired: the longest-increasing-subsequence used each pair's index in the array as its value, which is increasing by construction, so every pair was always kept and nothing was ever reported as moved.

The blind comparison still cannot be run here: it needs the same task performed in Cursor, Google Docs and Obsidian by an operator. It also now needs a starting document — checked against the project's own spec, 0 of 288 corpus files meet all five of its requirements at once.
The .docx corpus is public real-world documents. The 59 .docx files in ~/Downloads are personal and are deliberately not used.
